Title: Technical Advisory: AhsayCBS Exploitation Chain (CVE-2026-105133, CVE-2026-105134)
Context: Technical Advisory: AhsayCBS Exploitation Chain (CVE-2026-105133, CVE-2026-105134) #SMB Security #Enterprise Security #Ransomware #Threat Research By Martin Zugec / Oct 15, 2026...
Full Text:
[CRITICAL] | CVSS 10.0 (CVE-2026-105134, per VulDB) | Active exploitation confirmed, listed in CISA KEV | Patch immediately

TL;DR

Attackers are chaining two vulnerabilities in AhsayCBS, the server-side backup management platform of the Ahsay Cloud Backup Suite: CVE-2026-105133, an authentication flaw, and CVE-2026-105134, an OS command injection flaw rated CVSS 10.0 by VulDB. Every AhsayCBS v7 to v10 server that an attacker can reach, and that runs a build below v10.3.4.45 (v10) or v9.15.2.70 (v7, v8, v9), is exposed. That includes servers on the earlier patches v10.3.4.0 or v9.15.2.59, which the Ahsay announcement, October 2026 says did not fully fix the flaws. If you have already patched, you are not necessarily safe: verify the installed build, apply the new hotfix, reboot, and check for prior compromise. Patching closes the entry point but does not remove webshells or other access an attacker has already planted, and that access can sit unused for weeks before a ransomware or data theft attack. Bitdefender MDR has investigated multiple incidents at our customers through this chain since around 7 October 2026. For exact remediation steps, including how to identify affected systems and assess for prior compromise, see What To Do below.

Advisory History

15 October 2026: Initial publication, based on three Bitdefender MDR incident investigations. Vendor hotfixes are available, and both CVEs are listed in CISA KEV.

Situation

AhsayCBS is the server side of Ahsay’s backup product. It receives, stores and manages backups for the clients connected to it. Attackers are exploiting two flaws in its web-facing components in the wild. The timeline:

4 October 2026, 07:16 UTC: Both CVEs are published in the US National Vulnerability Database (NVD). Both entries state that a public exploit exists.

Around 7-8 October 2026: Bitdefender MDR’s first two incidents begin. They coincide with the first public reporting of exploitation and the first Ahsay advisories.

12 October 2026: Ahsay releases hotfixes (v10.3.4.45 for v10, v9.15.2.70 for v7, v8 and v9). The same advisory states that the earlier patches, v10.3.4.0 and v9.15.2.59, did not fully address the vulnerabilities.

14 October 2026: CISA adds both CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. KEV is the US government’s list of flaws with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, and federal agencies must fix listed flaws by a set deadline. MDR identifies a third incident the same day.

17 October 2026: CISA’s federal remediation deadline.

Bitdefender MDR investigations and the KEV listing both confirm exploitation. Some indicators in our incidents overlap with publicly reported activity. We do not attribute this activity to any named actor.

The NVD entries still list 10.3.4 as unaffected. The vendor’s later advisory supersedes that statement, and this advisory follows the vendor.

How it’s Exploited

Backup servers are a valuable foothold. They hold credentials for the systems they protect and the storage they write to, and they control the copies an organization relies on to recover. A ransomware operator wants to steal or destroy exactly that data before encrypting anything else. AhsayCBS exposes a management web service so administrators and clients can reach it, so on many deployments the server is reachable from the internet by design.

All three incidents Bitdefender MDR investigated began the same way, through a combination of the two CVEs. One flaw breaks authentication. Improper authentication means the server can be tricked into treating an unverified request as legitimate. The other is OS command injection, where text supplied by the attacker is executed as an operating system command on the server. Both NVD entries name the same argument, random, and neither flaw needs an account or any user action. MDR saw the two used together. NVD, however, scores the command injection as needing no privileges on its own, so an attacker may not need the full chain to run commands. A public exploit exists. CISA’s Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization (SSVC) is the model CISA uses to prioritize fixes, and it rates exploitation of both flaws as active and automatable.

Once inside, the attackers moved to confirm and test their access. In the first incident, they validated access through JSP webshells, which are small scripts planted on a web server that let an attacker run commands through ordinary web requests. They also staged PowerShell payloads, tried to stage payloads as command files (.cmd) in the shared C:\Users\Public folder, and tried to establish persistence, meaning a way back in that survives reboots and password changes. MDR analysts detected and blocked portions of this activity early. In the second incident, the attacker deployed JSP files (Java Server Pages, which act as webshells on this Java-based server) and again tried to stage command files in C:\Users\Public. The attacker then ran reconnaissance aimed at finding stored credentials, elevated a user account to SYSTEM (the highest privilege level on Windows), and used obfuscated PowerShell commands to install and configure OpenSSH, the standard remote-login service. A working SSH service would give an attacker a way back in that does not depend on the vulnerable web service, which is why patching alone does not end the incident. The attacker tried to establish persistence before being detected. In the third, MDR blocked and remediated the activity early in initial access. MDR credits three things: it identified known clusters of attacker behavior, the customer responded promptly, and configurations were reviewed quickly.

After that shared start, the incidents diverged. File names differed, the attackers abused different system tools and binaries, and the apparent objectives did not match. The Bitdefender MDR assessment is that the exploit chain was the constant, while file names, tools, and binaries changed from one incident to the next. Some indicators did overlap between the first two incidents, and the campaign appears to share some infrastructure: the C2 address 38.60.252[.]110 was the starting point of the two first incidents. Even so, a hash or file name from one incident may not reliably find the next one. The reliable signal is how the server behaves after the exploit fires. Combined with the differences between incidents, the shared infrastructure suggests a fluid situation in which several different actors may be using the same exploits. That is an assessment, not a finding, and it may change as more incidents surface.

Exposure conditions. Your server is exposed if two things are true. It runs AhsayCBS v7, v8, v9 or v10 below v9.15.2.70 (v7 to v9) or v10.3.4.45 (v10), and the attacker can reach its management web service. Servers on the earlier patches are not safe. An administrator who patched to v10.3.4.0 or v9.15.2.59 did the right thing at the time, but the vendor now says that fix was incomplete. The question to ask is not “did we patch?” The question is whether the server runs v10.3.4.45 or v9.15.2.70 or later.

Amplifying factors. VulDB, the CVE Numbering Authority, scores the command injection 10.0 under CVSS 3.1, the industry’s standard severity scale. A public exploit exists, and exploitation is rated automatable. The incomplete first patch leaves administrators believing they are covered. MDR’s assessment is that several actors may be using the chain. The credential reconnaissance in the second incident fits what backup servers hold.

Limiting factors. Exploitation requires network access to the management web service, so servers reachable only from internal networks carry less realistic exposure. MDR blocked one incident early in initial access and blocked part of the activity in another. MDR saw no encryption, data exfiltration or ransomware deployment. Ransomware remains a plausible risk because of the target type, but MDR did not observe it.

Confidence. This is observed in the wild, confirmed by first-party MDR investigations and corroborated by the KEV listing. We are not hedging on severity. This is internet-exposed, unauthenticated remote code execution with a public exploit, and in MDR’s assessment several different actors may be using it. That makes it a playbook case: continued opportunistic exploitation of unpatched and earlier-patched servers is near-certain. We are deliberately restrained on everything else. Three incidents cannot establish who is behind this, how many groups are involved, or what they ultimately want.

If you have confirmed exposure, skip ahead to What To Do.

How it Works

Public disclosure of the mechanism is limited. Everything below comes from the NVD entries and Bitdefender MDR observations, and nothing here speculates on root cause. Each flaw carries a CWE classification. CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration) is the standard catalog of software weakness types.

CVE-2026-105133 (improper authentication, CWE-287). The flaw is in the checkSysPwd function of the API component, in ApiStructsAction.java. Manipulating the random argument results in improper authentication. It can be exploited remotely, with no privileges and no user interaction.

CVE-2026-105134 (OS command injection, CWE-77 and CWE-78). The flaw is in the Replication Receiver component, the offsite store that synchronizes backup data from one or more AhsayCBS servers (Ahsay, “CBS v9 Replication Guide”, August 2025). The affected endpoint is /rps/api/json/UpdateReceivers.do. Manipulating the same random argument leads to OS command injection, again remotely and with no privileges or user interaction.

Why is this possible? NVD classifies the two as different weaknesses: improper authentication in CVE-2026-105133 and OS command injection in CVE-2026-105134, both reached by manipulating the random argument. Ahsay has not published why the first patches fell short, and we will not guess.

Scores. VulDB assigned all scores below as the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), the organization that issued these CVE IDs. NVD reports them but has not published scores of its own.

CVE

CVSS 3.1

CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-105133

7.3 High (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L)

5.5 Medium

CVE-2026-105134

10.0 Critical (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H)

9.3 Critical

The 105134 vector describes a flaw that is reachable over the network (AV:N), has low attack complexity (AC:L), needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N/UI:N), and has high impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability. The scope change (S:C) means a successful attack affects resources beyond the vulnerable component itself.

Neither NVD nor MDR states what privilege level the injected commands run with, and we do not claim one.

Observed staging. In MDR’s incidents, the attackers staged follow-on PowerShell scripts on a subdomain of a public static-site hosting service. Staging means placing payloads somewhere the compromised server can download them in a later step. The observed URLs were hxxps://captcha-eyw[.]pages[.]dev/challenges.ps1 and hxxps://captcha-eyw[.]pages[.]dev/install.ps1. In the first two incidents, the attackers also tried to stage payloads as .cmd files in C:\Users\Public, a folder every local user can write to, which makes it a common drop location. In the second incident, obfuscated PowerShell commands installed and configured OpenSSH. This advisory publishes no file hashes or webshell paths, because the MDR data does not support a stable set.

What To Do

The steps below expand on the immediate actions summarized in the TL;DR.

1. Identify Exposure

List every AhsayCBS server you run, including any a service provider operates for you. Check the installed build on each one. In the AhsayCBS web console, go to System Settings > License > Update License, which shows the Product Version. Ahsay documents this path for AhsayCBS 7.5 and above on all platforms (Ahsay, “KB5009”, September 2025). Versions appear as four-part numbers, for example 9.8.5.1, so compare the full number against v10.3.4.45 or v9.15.2.70.

A server is fixed only if it runs v10.3.4.45 or later (v10), or v9.15.2.70 or later (v7, v8, v9). “We already patched” does not answer the question. A server on v10.3.4.0 or v9.15.2.59 has the earlier patch and is still vulnerable. Update it and check it for compromise.

Then confirm whether the management web service is reachable from the internet or other untrusted networks. Review the firewall and network address translation (NAT) rules, which map outside addresses to the server, and test from an external vantage point.

2. Patch or Mitigate

Apply the hotfix for your version from the Ahsay announcement (vendor support account may be required): v10.3.4.45 for v10, or v9.15.2.70 for v7, v8 and v9. A hotfix is a targeted update released outside the normal release schedule. Reboot the server afterward, as the same advisory instructs.

The announcement lists no workaround. If you cannot apply the hotfix immediately, Bitdefender recommends limiting access to the management web service to known administrative networks until you can. This is our recommendation, not vendor guidance. It reduces exposure but does not remove it.

Patching closes the entry point. It does not remove webshells, staged scripts or persistence an attacker has already put in place, so continue to step 3 whatever your patch status.

3. Assess for Prior Compromise

Search from at least 4 October 2026, the date the CVEs were published in NVD.

File names and tools varied between incidents, so hunt for behavior rather than specific artifacts:

New or recently modified JSP or other script files in the AhsayCBS web application directories that you did not deploy

Command shells or PowerShell launched as child processes of the AhsayCBS service

PowerShell downloading scripts from external hosting services, including the staging URLs in Indicators of Compromise

Command (.cmd) files in C:\Users\Public that you did not create

OpenSSH installed or configured on a server that never ran it, especially through obfuscated PowerShell, and user accounts whose privileges changed since 4 October

New Windows services, scheduled tasks or other persistence created on the server since 4 October

Outbound connections from the server to the C2 addresses listed below. C2 (command and control) servers are attacker-run machines that compromised systems contact for instructions.

Access to credential stores or configuration files holding stored passwords

If you find signs of compromise, treat the server as untrusted. Rotate the credentials stored on that server or reachable from it: AhsayCBS administrator accounts, credentials for the backup storage destinations it writes to, the service accounts it runs under, and any domain credentials used or cached on the host. This advisory alone is not a reason to rotate credentials that have no path to the server.

4. Monitor Ongoing

Keep monitoring the server’s behavior after patching: child processes of the backup service, new script files in web directories, files appearing in C:\Users\Public, new remote-access services such as OpenSSH, new services and scheduled tasks, and unexpected outbound connections. Bitdefender MDR’s assessment is that several different actors may be using this chain, so a static blocklist from one incident will not cover the next. Keep checking the Ahsay advisory for further updates, because the first fix has already been superseded once.

5. Do Not Wait for Something to Happen

Quiet is not the same as clean. Our ransomware research describes “delayed attacks”: a gap of days or weeks between initial access and the next stage, and a manual phase that can run for weeks or months after an automated first wave (Bitdefender TechZone, “Stopping Ransomware”). Initial access brokers, criminals who sell entry to compromised networks, often hand the access to ransomware groups with no link to the original intrusion. A webshell or a new remote-access service that no one has used yet is not harmless: the attacker may be holding the access for later, using it to stage cryptominers, or selling it to another group. Bitdefender MDR has not determined the objective in these incidents, and we do not claim one. Plan on the assumption that an attacker who got in is waiting to use it.

So if your server was exposed and unpatched at any point since 4 October 2026, do not treat the absence of visible damage as the all-clear. Complete the compromise assessment in step 3 even if nothing looks wrong, and treat any finding as an active intrusion, not a leftover.

Title: Who’s Watching AI? The Visibility Gap Security Teams Need to Close
Context: 8% of IT and cybersecurity professionals have only partial visibility into employee AI use
Full Text:
AI adoption isn't waiting for security teams.

Employees are experimenting with new tools. Business leaders are pushing teams to use AI to work faster. Applications are adding AI functionality. AI agents are accessing files, connecting to tools, and taking action as if they were employees.

This has tremendous potential.

But there's also a fundamental cybersecurity problem: Do you know what AI is doing inside your organization, or is it a growing blind spot?

That's the question at the center of a new episode of Cybercrime: From the Frontline, Who’s Watching AI? Managing Innovation Without Losing Control.

Watch or listen to the full conversation to hear Bitdefender experts explore how organizations can embrace AI innovation while managing its risks.

How Many Organizations Lack Full AI Visibility?

The 2026 Bitdefender Cybersecurity Assessment reveals that 44.8% of IT and cybersecurity professionals have only partial visibility into employee AI use. Another roughly 3% report having no visibility at all.

The independent research surveyed 1,200 IT and cybersecurity professionals across six countries and shows how widespread the lack of AI visibility and control has become. And the challenge is growing because employees have powerful incentives to experiment. AI can accelerate development, automate repetitive work, analyze information, and help meet increasingly aggressive productivity expectations.

Has Shadow IT Become Shadow AI?

Shadow AI introduces similar challenges to Shadow IT, but with potentially greater consequences.

With Shadow IT, an employee installs an unauthorized application. A department adopts a cloud service without consulting IT. Someone stores corporate information in a personal file-sharing account.

With Shadow AI, an employee might use a personal AI account instead of an approved enterprise platform. Someone could paste confidential information into a free AI service. An approved application might gain new AI capabilities through an update.

In each case, sensitive information could move somewhere security teams didn't anticipate. That's particularly concerning given that data leakage into large language models ranks among the leading AI-related concerns identified in the 2026 Cybersecurity Assessment.

According to experts on the podcast episode, AI adoption often happens without IT or security oversight, making visibility an enterprise-wide responsibility.

Why Is AI Becoming an Identity Problem?

Traditional generative AI responds to requests. Agentic AI can interact with tools, access files, connect to services, write code, and take actions. During the podcast, our experts suggest thinking about these agents as non-human identities operating inside the organization.

That raises important questions:

Which agents are operating in your environment?

What data can they access?

Which tools can they use?

What actions are they permitted to take?

And what happens if an agent is manipulated?

The podcast also explores prompt injection, where malicious instructions embedded within content can influence an AI system into performing unintended actions. If an agent has access to corporate systems, the question isn't simply whether you trust the AI.

What Does AI Visibility Look Like Today?

A simple inventory isn't enough. To achieve AI visibility, organizations must be able to identify the AI services and agents operating across their environments. Security teams need context on those tools, including their capabilities, permissions, connections, potential risks, and the endpoints they affect.

They also need to distinguish sanctioned AI use from unknown or potentially dangerous activity. Without that understanding, organizations risk applying blanket restrictions that frustrate employees or overlooking exposures that genuinely threaten the business.

Visibility provides the foundation for prioritizing risk and applying appropriate controls.

What Kinds of Tools Create AI Visibility and Control?

Organizations increasingly need specialized capabilities that discover AI usage, assess exposure, and translate security policies into action. One example is Bitdefender GravityZone AI Visibility and Control, which helps security teams identify more than 700 AI tools, including chatbots, coding assistants, local LLMs, agents, MCP servers, and AI-enabled applications. It creates a centralized inventory and helps prioritize findings based on risk and business context.

Importantly, GravityZone goes beyond discovery. Security teams can review and investigate findings, then use integrated controls to allow, restrict, or block AI activity. For existing GravityZone customers, these capabilities operate through the same agent and console, helping organizations manage AI exposure without adding another disconnected security tool.

How Can AI Governance Keep Pace With AI Adoption?

Technology is part of the answer, but AI governance must also become part of acceptable-use policies, employee education, procurement reviews, third-party risk assessments, and conversations between security and business leaders.

Some organizations are establishing dedicated AI steering committees. Others are incorporating AI into existing security and risk governance. The structure matters less than the outcome: security needs to participate in AI adoption decisions before deploying new tools.

Can Organizations Innovate Without Losing Control?

According to the podcast episode's experts, organizations can continue AI innovation without losing control, but only with a sound strategy. Instead of putting the brakes on AI adoption, organizations should make approved AI easier to use safely, educate employees about the risks of unsanctioned tools, use technology to track where sensitive information moves, and establish controls based on actual usage.

As AI agents become more capable, organizations must also understand and constrain agent permissions, just as they would for human identities.

Together, these measures can help make AI innovation sustainable.

Title: The Sovereign Advantage: Why MSPs Who Move First Will Control the Board
Context: Sovereignty is achieved only when all three are in place
Full Text:
In chess, the first player to move gains more than a step. They shape how the board develops from that point on. Digital sovereignty works the same way. MSPs that make their sovereign move now build an advantage that could decide who leads the market.

That is the idea behind our webinar, The Sovereign Advantage: Move First to Control the Board, where Alina Drăgănescu (Deputy GM of the Business Solutions Group and SVP of Business Operations, Bitdefender) and Nadine Pilote (Managing Director, Septeo IT Solutions) join Mia Thompson (Senior Product Marketing Manager, Bitdefender) to discuss what it takes to build a sovereign, compliance-ready security practice.

Key webinar takeaways to expect

Understand the difference between data residency and data sovereignty.

Explore why cybersecurity sovereignty requires three forms of control working together: data, technical, and operational.

See how Bitdefender takes a unified approach that is European-built, European-operated, and EU-governed.

Learn how MSPs can add a sovereign service tier for regulated customers without changing their operating model.

Gain clarity on the ways Bitdefender EU Sovereign MDR brings sovereignty into security operations, with monitoring, investigation, and response delivered within the EU.

Why Does a Cybersecurity Platform Hold More Than Security Data?

A modern cybersecurity platform collects signals from across the organization, so it holds one of a client's richest operational datasets, not just security events.

Twenty years ago, security tools had a narrow view. Today, a cybersecurity platform brings together signals from endpoints, servers, identities, email, cloud workloads, networks, SaaS applications, and increasingly AI-powered tools. It does not just see security events. It sees how an organization operates.

That changes the questions buyers ask. They no longer stop at "can this platform protect us?" They want to know where the information is stored, who governs access to it, which laws apply, and who ultimately controls it?

What Are the Three Dimensions of Cybersecurity Sovereignty?

Cybersecurity sovereignty requires three forms of control that work together: data sovereignty (control over security data), technical sovereignty (control over the technology), and operational sovereignty (control over operations). Sovereignty is achieved only when all three are in place.

1. Data sovereignty: control over security data

Security telemetry, logs, and incident data stay protected under European governance, with EU-based storage and processing, controlled access, and trusted, certified sovereign European cloud infrastructure.

2. Technical sovereignty: control over the technology

The cybersecurity platform itself is governed under European jurisdiction, built on European-designed technology and the EU legal framework, with reduced exposure to non-EU legal authority.

3. Operational sovereignty: control over operations

Security services are delivered from the EU, with monitoring, investigation, and response staying within it.

A provider can store data in Europe, but without technical and operational sovereignty, jurisdictional risk may remain.

How Does Bitdefender Approach Cybersecurity Sovereignty?

Bitdefender takes a unified approach that combines data, technical, and operational control, delivered as European-built, European-operated, and EU-governed cybersecurity.

The outcome is not simply European data residency. It combines data, technical, and operational control, backed by European infrastructure, governance, and cybersecurity technology.

Bitdefender is headquartered and governed in the EU, and it develops its technology under EU jurisdiction. GravityZone is available through sovereign cloud deployments with European partners, including OVHcloud in France, Secunet in Germany, and Aruba in Italy.

How Can MSPs Add a Sovereign Service Tier Without Changing Their Operating Model

MSPs can keep their scalable operating model and add a sovereign service tier for regulated or sensitive customers, all on the same unified GravityZone platform. Sovereignty does not have to be an all-or-nothing infrastructure decision.

A strong approach is to start by understanding your customers:

Identify which industries, clients, datasets, and workloads carry the highest jurisdictional risk.

Define the level of sovereignty each one needs.

Introduce a sovereign tier where it creates genuine customer and commercial value.

What Is Bitdefender EU Sovereign MDR?

EU Sovereign MDR is AI-enabled, human-led 24/7 Managed Detection and Response delivered entirely within the EU sovereign operating model. It brings sovereignty into security operations, which matters because customers increasingly ask who can access their data during an investigation, and where the team doing that work sits. This is where Bitdefender MDR becomes a leading solution for sovereign-ready service delivery.

What makes it sovereign:

24/7/365 MDR delivered by EU experts from an EU-based SOC

All monitoring, investigations, and incident response remain within the EU

No follow-the-sun handoffs or case escalations outside the EU

Threat research, malware analysis, and detection engineering remain within the EU

AI-assisted investigations use sovereign-hosted LLMs, so customer data is never processed by public AI services

People, processes, tooling, and service delivery stay under EU control, even during incident response. For MSPs, it also means growing a security service without building a full security operations center themselves.

What Does "Moving First" Mean for MSPs?

Moving first means making the sovereignty choice before you are forced to, and acting before sovereignty becomes a mandatory line in every customer tender.

Both speakers close on this idea. For Alina, moving first looks like this:

Focus on the customers for whom jurisdiction matters most.

Build a sovereign-ready service option.

Train your commercial and technical teams to explain it.

Put processes in place to deliver it consistently.

The advantage is not simply saying you offer sovereign cybersecurity. It is being able to demonstrate how it works, where the data is processed, who governs the technology, and how customers stay protected without sacrificing operational effectiveness.

What Will You Learn in the Webinar?

The Sovereign Advantage: Move First to Control the Board is designed for MSPs and MSSPs. Watch it live or on demand to hear a practical discussion of:

How Bitdefender approaches sovereign-ready deployment, and what it delivers for MSPs in practice

The three dimensions of cybersecurity sovereignty: data, technical, and operational

How EU Sovereign MDR extends sovereignty into security operations

How to build a staged, defensible path to sovereignty without an all-or-nothing migration

Join us, October 27, 4:00 PM CET. Available on demand after the live session.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is digital sovereignty in cybersecurity?Digital sovereignty in cybersecurity is control over the security data, the technology, and the operations that protect an organization. It goes beyond where data is stored and covers who governs the technology, which legal jurisdiction applies, who can access the data, and who runs the security operations.

Is data residency enough to be sovereign?No. Data residency only answers where data is stored. Sovereignty also depends on legal jurisdiction, governance, and who can access, process, or compel access to the data. A provider can store data in Europe, but without technical and operational sovereignty, jurisdictional risk may remain.

What are the three dimensions of cybersecurity sovereignty?They are data sovereignty (control over security data), technical sovereignty (control over the technology), and operational sovereignty (control over operations). Sovereignty is achieved only when all three work together.

What is EU Sovereign MDR?EU Sovereign MDR is Bitdefender's AI-enabled, human-led 24/7 Managed Detection and Response, delivered entirely within the EU sovereign operating model. Monitoring, investigations, and incident response stay within the EU, with no follow-the-sun handoffs or case escalations outside it.

Do MSPs need to rebuild their operating model to offer sovereign services?No. An MSP can keep its scalable operating model and add a sovereign service tier for regulated or sensitive customers on the same unified GravityZone platform.

Why is sovereignty becoming a buying criterion for European organizations?Regulated buyers increasingly ask who can be compelled to access their data and under whose laws, not only where it is stored. In 2026, NIS2, DORA, and the Cyber Resilience Act move from awareness to active enforcement, which makes the question a live one.

Title: The Cybersecurity Optimism Gap: When Leaders and Frontline Teams See Different Realities
Context: Based on an independent survey of 1,200 IT and cybersecurity professionals across six countries, the report found that IT and security leaders rated their organization’s...
Full Text:
Security leaders and frontline practitioners can look at the same organization, controls, and dashboards, and reach different conclusions about how well cybersecurity is working.

One side sees strategic progress, stronger alignment, and investments beginning to pay off. The other sees the alerts, workarounds, staffing constraints, and gaps that remain unresolved beneath the strategy.

The 2026 Bitdefender Cybersecurity Assessment reveals how consistently those perspectives diverge. Based on an independent survey of 1,200 IT and cybersecurity professionals across six countries, the report found that IT and security leaders rated their organization’s cybersecurity posture 8% higher, on average, than frontline practitioners did.

This is a cybersecurity optimism gap, and leaving it unaddressed can affect priorities, investments, and risk.

Leaders vs. Practitioners: Do We Have Internal AI Visibility?

A major priority of most organizations right now is gaining visibility into internal AI use. This is also where the cybersecurity assessment uncovered the biggest perception gap between leadership and the frontline. Among managers and leaders, 57.8% say their organization has full visibility into the AI tools employees are using. However, only 45.9% of practitioners agreed, an 11.9-percentage-point gap the cybersecurity assessment uncovered.

“One of the hardest questions I could probably ask an organization today is, ‘Can you confidently tell me every AI platform your employees are using?’ For many organizations, the answer is no,” says Josh Armstrong, Senior Manager of the Bitdefender Global SOC.

What’s driving the perception gap here? Leaders may believe AI governance rests on a reasonably complete inventory, while practitioners closer to endpoints and user activity may see unknown applications, browser extensions, coding assistants, agents, and data connections keep emerging.

If leadership believes visibility is stronger than it actually is, the organization may underestimate its Shadow AI exposure, overestimate the reach of existing policy, or delay investments in tools that can identify internal AI use.

Leaders vs. Practitioners: Who Is More Optimistic About Security Improvements?

The cybersecurity assessment found that 74% of leaders expressed confidence in their organization’s ability to close security gaps, compared with 67.1% of frontline practitioners, a 6.9-point difference.

To leadership, a funded initiative, approved roadmap, or newly deployed platform can represent meaningful progress. Practitioners see it differently, says Bitdefender Technical Solutions Director, Martin Zugec. “Looking at this from the view of a security architect, you pay less attention to what is already secure, and you think more about everything that is unsecure that remains in front of you.”

Both perceptions can be valid at the same time.

Leaders vs Practitioners: Is Cybersecurity Aligned with the Business?

Leaders and managers were 7.4 points more likely to say cybersecurity is aligned with business objectives: 72.8% of managers said the two were aligned, compared with 65.4% of frontline practitioners, according to the 2026 Bitdefender Cybersecurity Assessment.

Executives and managers often experience alignment through budgets, governance meetings, and strategic plans. Frontline teams experience it through operating decisions: whether security requirements are introduced early, business owners accept necessary controls, and teams receive enough time and resources to implement them.

Alignment written into a strategy is important. Alignment experienced in daily operations is what makes it real.

Leaders vs Practitioners: Can We Address the Security Skills Gap?

The perception gap narrows when respondents consider workforce development. Nearly three-quarters of leaders, 73.7%, said their organization understood which internal cybersecurity skills it needed to develop. Among practitioners, 68.7% agreed, creating a five-point gap.

Knowing which skills are needed is only the beginning. Frontline teams also see whether employees have time to train, whether expertise is applied, and whether staffing levels allow those skills to make a difference.

This is where workforce strategy meets operational capacity. A skills plan may look complete from above while still feeling out of reach to the people expected to carry it out.

Leaders vs Practitioners: Is Compliance Overwhelming?

Compliance adds pressure to the majority of those working within cybersecurity.

According to the cybersecurity assessment, 65.2% of leaders and managers say compliance feels overwhelming, but that number drops to 58.1% when it comes to practitioners. This is a 7 point perception gap.

This may reflect leadership responsibilities for interpreting requirements, demonstrating accountability, reporting to boards, and directing limited resources. Practitioners may feel the operational burden of compliance, while leaders feel its organizational and reputational weight.

What Overall Factors Lead to the Cybersecurity Optimism Gap?

“The gap will continue to be a challenge, because the people on the front line are seeing a lot more of the day-to-day activities, so they understand more of every single gap,” says Nicholas Jackson, Director of Cybersecurity Services at Bitdefender. “The industry is still in a position where a lot of the data that the frontline workers are providing to managers are either piecemeal, incomplete, or even based on assumptions. As a result, I think managers often end up with a false sense of confidence.”

How Can I Read the Complete Cybersecurity Assessment?
